tools.medicare-cost-calculator.guide.how: Part A is premium-free if you (or your spouse) worked and paid Medicare taxes for more than 40 quarters (10 years). With 30-39 quarters, you pay $311/month. Fewer than 30 quarters: $565/month. Part A has a $1,736 deductible per benefit period (2026), plus daily copays beyond 60 days.

Part B covers doctor visits, outpatient care, preventive services, medical equipment, ambulance services, mental health, and some home health care. The 2026 standard premium is $202.90/month with a $283 annual deductible. After the deductible, you typically pay 20% coinsurance with no out-of-pocket maximum.

Part D averages about $39/month in 2026. Starting in 2025, the Inflation Reduction Act set the Part D out-of-pocket cap at $2,000 per year ($2,100 in 2026). Once you reach this cap, you pay $0 for covered drugs for the rest of the year.

IRMAA (Income-Related Monthly Adjustment Amount) is a surcharge added to Part B and Part D premiums for higher-income beneficiaries. It is based on your MAGI from 2 years ago (2026 premiums use 2024 income). IRMAA kicks in starting at $109,001 for singles and $218,001 for married filing jointly.
tools.medicare-cost-calculator.guide.tip: Part B: a 10% premium surcharge for every full 12 months you were eligible but did not enroll — permanently. Part D: 1% of the base premium for every uncovered month ($0.39/month in 2026) — also permanent. These penalties add up fast: delaying Part B by 3 years means paying 30% more for life.
tools.mortgage-payoff-calculator.metadat: Calculate how much extra monthly payments can shorten your term and save in interest.
How can I pay off my mortgage faster?

Strategies: 1) Biweekly payments (one extra payment per year), 2) add 1/12 to each monthly payment, 3) make one extra lump-sum payment per year, 4) round payments up to the next $100. Any method saves thousands in interest.
Should I refinance or make extra payments?

Refinancing is worth it if rates are more than 1% lower. Otherwise, extra payments are better — no closing costs and immediate interest savings. Refinancing resets your term (unless you choose a 15-year).
How do extra payments save interest?

Extra payments directly reduce the principal, shrinking the amount that accrues interest. A $100 extra payment on a 30-year, 4% loan saves about $180 in interest. Over time, the compounding savings are significant.
Some loans have them — especially in the early years. Check your promissory note. Most conventional loans have no penalty. If the penalty exceeds the savings, avoid extra payments until the penalty period ends.

tools.net-worth-percentile-calculator.fa: What is the median net worth in the U.S.?

The median U.S. household net worth is approximately $192,700. The average (mean) is much higher at about $1,060,000 because extremely wealthy households pull the average up. Median is a better measure of the 'typical' American's wealth.
What net worth makes you top 1%?

A net worth of roughly $13 million or more puts you in the top 1% of U.S. households. The threshold varies by age: for under-35 households it's around $1.5M, while for 55-64 year olds it's around $15M.
What should my net worth be at my age?

A common guideline is to have 1x your annual salary saved by 30, 3x by 40, 6x by 50, 8x by 60, and 10x by 67. However, these are rough targets. The median net worth by age group gives a more realistic picture of where Americans actually stand.
Does net worth include home equity?

Yes. Net worth equals total assets minus total debts. Assets include home equity, retirement accounts, savings, investments, vehicles, and other property. Debts include mortgages, student loans, auto loans, credit cards, and any other liabilities.
Why is average net worth so much higher than median?

The top 10% of households hold about 70% of all wealth. A few extremely wealthy families (with net worths in the billions) dramatically pull the average upward, making it unrepresentative of typical Americans. The median (50th percentile) is the point where exactly half of households have more and half have less.
How does net worth vary by age?

Net worth generally increases with age due to accumulated savings, home equity, and investment growth. The median rises from about $39,000 for under-35 to $410,000 for ages 65-74, then declines slightly to $336,000 for 75+ as retirees draw down savings.

tools.ohms-law-calculator.faqs.0.answer: Ohm's Law states that voltage = current × resistance (V = IR). It describes the relationship between voltage, current, and resistance in a circuit. If you know two of them, you can calculate the third.
tools.ohms-law-calculator.faqs.1.answer: Power (watts) = voltage × current (P = VI). Using Ohm's Law to substitute: P = I²R or P = V²/R. This is used for electrical systems and appliance ratings.
tools.ohms-law-calculator.faqs.2.questio: What happens to current if resistance increases?
tools.ohms-law-calculator.faqs.2.answer: At constant voltage, current decreases as resistance increases (I = V/R). Doubling the resistance means half the current. This is why long extension cords (higher resistance) reduce current to devices.
tools.ohms-law-calculator.faqs.3.answer: It is the foundation of all electrical engineering. Designing circuits, selecting fuses, wiring, and ensuring appliances receive the right power all rely on Ohm's Law. Without it, electrical systems would be unpredictable and dangerous.

tools.personal-injury-calculator.metadat: Estimate personal injury settlement amounts based on medical bills, lost wages, and a pain multiplier.
How are personal injury settlements calculated?

Insurance companies use the "multiplier method" as a starting point. Your total medical expenses are multiplied by a factor (1.5x for minor injuries, up to 10x for catastrophic injuries) to estimate pain and suffering. Lost wages and property damage are added separately. The result is then adjusted by your percentage of fault according to your state's negligence rules and is limited by the defendant's insurance policy limits.
What is the pain and suffering multiplier?

The multiplier is a number (typically 1.5 to 10) applied to your medical bills to estimate non-economic damages such as pain, suffering, mental anguish, and loss of enjoyment of life. Minor soft tissue injuries use 1.5-3x, moderate injuries like fractures use 3-5x, serious injuries requiring surgery use 5-7x, and catastrophic or permanent injuries use 7-10x or higher.
Comparative negligence reduces your settlement by your percentage of fault. In "pure comparative" states (like CA and NY), you can recover even at 99% fault. In "modified comparative" states, you are barred from recovery at 50% or 51% fault, depending on the state. In "pure contributory" states (AL, MD, NC, VA, DC), you are barred from any recovery even at just 1% fault.
How do insurance policy limits affect my settlement?

The defendant's insurance policy limits are usually the practical ceiling on your recovery, regardless of your case's theoretical value. If your case is worth $500,000 but the defendant only has $50,000 in liability coverage, you will likely only collect $50,000 unless the defendant has substantial personal assets. Your own underinsured motorist (UIM) coverage can make up the difference.
Does having surgery increase my settlement?

Yes, significantly. Cases involving surgery typically settle for 2-5 times more than cases with conservative treatment only. Surgery provides objective evidence of injury severity and proves that less invasive treatment was insufficient.
What if I have a pre-existing condition?

Under the "eggshell plaintiff" doctrine, the defendant takes you as they find you — if a minor collision causes serious injury because of a pre-existing condition, the defendant is still liable. However, insurance adjusters will argue your treatment was for the pre-existing condition rather than the accident. The key is proving the accident caused a flare-up or worsening of your condition.
Do most states cap pain and suffering damages?

No. Most states do not cap non-economic damages in general personal injury cases. Only about 4 states have enforceable general personal injury damage caps (CO, MD, OH, TN). More states cap damages specifically for medical malpractice cases, but those caps do not apply to car accidents, slip and falls, or other general injury claims.
Should I hire a lawyer for my injury claim?

Research consistently shows that represented claimants recover 3-3.5 times more than unrepresented claimants, even after attorney fees (typically 33-40% on contingency). For minor soft tissue injuries with clear liability and low medical bills, you may be able to handle the claim yourself. For moderate to severe injuries, surgery cases, liability disputes, or cases involving permanent impairment, an attorney will almost certainly increase your net recovery.
tools.personal-injury-calculator.guide.w: How the Personal Injury Calculator Works
This calculator uses the multiplier method to estimate your personal injury settlement, the standard approach insurance adjusters and personal injury attorneys use to evaluate claims.
tools.personal-injury-calculator.guide.h: Your medical expenses (called "specials") are multiplied by a factor based on injury severity to estimate pain and suffering ("generals"). Lost wages and property damage are added as separate economic damages. Formula: settlement = medical bills + (medical bills × multiplier) + lost wages + property damage

Your state's negligence laws determine how fault affects your recovery. Pure comparative negligence states allow recovery at any fault level (reduced proportionally). Modified comparative states bar recovery at 50% or 51% fault. Five jurisdictions (AL, MD, NC, VA, DC) use pure contributory negligence, which bars any recovery even at 1% fault.
tools.personal-injury-calculator.guide.t: Insurance companies use proprietary software (like Colossus) that considers hundreds of factors. The multiplier method is a simplified version of what that software does. Actual settlements depend on the specific facts of your case, the quality of evidence, the jurisdiction, the judge or jury, whether you have an attorney, and the defendant's insurance coverage.

tools.save-vs-rap-calculator.faqs.0.answ: RAP (Random Additional Payments) are extra payments made beyond your regular loan payment. They directly reduce the principal, accelerating repayment and saving interest. Same as extra payments, but the terminology varies by lender.
tools.save-vs-rap-calculator.faqs.1.ques: What is the difference between RAP and extra payments?
tools.save-vs-rap-calculator.faqs.1.answ: None — they are the same thing. RAP is just the term some lenders use. Both reduce the principal, shorten the loan term, and save interest.
tools.save-vs-rap-calculator.faqs.2.ques: Should I save or pay RAP?
tools.save-vs-rap-calculator.faqs.2.answ: If your loan rate is higher than your savings rate, pay RAP. If the loan rate is lower than investment returns, invest the difference. Rule of thumb: if the rate is > 6%, prioritize the debt; if it is < 4%, prioritize investing.
tools.save-vs-rap-calculator.faqs.3.ques: How does RAP affect my loan?
tools.save-vs-rap-calculator.faqs.3.answ: RAP reduces the outstanding balance, lowering future interest. Some lenders recalculate your payment (lowering it), while others shorten the term (keeping payments the same). Designate the payment to be applied to principal.

tools.self-employment-tax-calculator.faq: Self-employment tax is the Social Security and Medicare tax for self-employed workers. In 2026, the rate is 15.3% of net earnings (12.4% Social Security + 2.9% Medicare). You pay both the employer and employee shares.
How much income is subject to self-employment tax?
Social Security tax applies to net earnings up to $176,100 (2026). Medicare tax applies to all net earnings. An additional 0.9% Medicare tax applies above $200,000 (single).
Yes. You can deduct the employer-equivalent portion (7.65% of net earnings) as an above-the-line deduction. This reduces your income tax, but not the self-employment tax itself.
Do LLC owners pay self-employment tax?

Yes, unless you elect S corporation status. A single-member LLC is treated as a disregarded entity — you pay self-employment tax. S corp owners pay FICA tax only on their salary (not distributions), which can save money.

tools.small-claims-court-calculator.meta: Estimate small claims court filing and service fees based on your claim amount.
tools.small-claims-court-calculator.faqs: Small claims court is a simplified legal process for resolving disputes involving relatively small amounts of money. The rules are designed for people without lawyers — hearings are informal, there is no jury, and cases are usually decided the same day. Amount limits range from $2,500 (Kentucky) to $25,000 (Tennessee, Delaware). Filing fees are typically $25-$150.
Do I need a lawyer in small claims court?

In most cases, no — in 13 states (including California, Arizona, Colorado, Michigan, and Washington), attorneys are actually prohibited from representing parties in small claims court. The court is designed for self-representation. However, in states that allow lawyers, one side having an attorney can put the other at a disadvantage.
What is the statute of limitations?

The statute of limitations is the deadline for filing a claim after an event occurs. It varies by state and claim type. For example, Kentucky gives you only 1 year for personal injury claims, while Maine allows 6 years. Written contracts usually have longer deadlines (3-15 years) than personal injury claims (1-6 years). Missing this deadline means your case is dismissed.
What if my claim exceeds the small claims limit?

You have three options: (1) reduce your claim to the small claims limit and waive the rest, (2) file in regular civil court (more expensive and complex), or (3) in some states, split the claim into multiple cases (though many states prohibit this). If the excess is small relative to civil court costs, option 1 is usually the best choice.
Can I appeal a small claims decision?

It depends on your state. Most states allow either party to appeal, usually within 10-30 days. California and Massachusetts only allow the defendant to appeal. Arizona does not allow small claims appeals at all. Appeals are usually "trial de novo" (a brand-new trial) in a higher court.
Where do I file a small claims case?

Almost always in the county or district where the defendant lives or does business, or where the incident occurred (where the contract was signed, where the property was damaged, etc.). Filing in the wrong location can result in dismissal.
Which states have the highest and lowest limits?

Highest: Tennessee and Delaware ($25,000), Texas and Utah ($20,000), Georgia, Minnesota, and North Dakota ($15,000). Lowest: Kentucky ($2,500), Arizona and Mississippi ($3,500), Nebraska ($3,900), Kansas ($4,000). California allows $12,500 for individuals but only $6,250 for businesses.
How long does small claims court take?

It typically takes 30-75 days from filing to the hearing. The hearing itself usually takes 15-60 minutes, and you get a decision that day or within a few days. If you win, collecting the judgment can take longer — the court does not collect it for you.
